slides.title: Secondary Storage Management: Managing secondary storage
slides.body:
Secondary Storage Management: Managing secondary storage
RAID Concept: Motivation for RAID
RAID Levels - I: RAID 0 (striping) & RAID 1 (mirroring)
RAID Levels - II: RAID 5 (distributed parity) & RAID 6; RAID 10 (nested)
Trade-offs & Reliability: Performance, redundancy & cost; Storage reliability & data protection

slides.title: Secondary Storage Management
slides.body: Secondary Storage Management

slides.title: Heading: Storage Management Layers
slides.body:
Subheading: From Device To File
Content:
Secondary storage management coordinates physical devices, media and logical layers so data stays available, fast and reliable.
Devices: raw disks, SSDs, tapes accessed via controllers
Media: sector geometry mapped to logical block addresses
Partition/volume layer: fixed regions with mount points
Array layer: JBOD concatenates capacity, spanning extends one volume
File system layer: naming, allocation, directories sit above

slides.title: Heading: Volumes And Monitoring
slides.body:
Subheading: Pooling And Tracking Health
Content:
A logical volume manager pools physical disks into resizable volumes, while ongoing monitoring tracks health and capacity before problems occur.
PVs pool into a VG, then sliced into LVs
Online resize and point-in-time snapshots without reformatting
SMART firmware metrics predict drive failure before loss
Capacity, throughput and IOPS thresholds trigger alerts early

slides.title: Heading: Volumes And Monitoring
slides.body:
Subheading: Analogy
Analogy:
A common water tank fed by several borewells lets pipes of any needed size draw from one pool — just as an LVM pools multiple physical disks into a volume group from which logical volumes of any size are carved.

slides.title: RAID Concept
slides.body: RAID Concept

slides.title: Heading: Single Disk Limits
slides.body:
Subheading: Three Bottlenecks
Content:
A single disk hits a ceiling on how much it can hold, how fast it can be read, and how long it survives before failing.
Capacity ceiling: largest single disk still bounds total storage
Performance ceiling: one disk gives one head's IOPS and throughput
Reliability risk: any single disk is one point of failure
Plain concatenation (JBOD) adds only capacity, not speed or safety

slides.title: Heading: RAID Defined
slides.body:
Subheading: Striping Plus Redundancy
Content:
RAID combines several physical disks into one logical unit managed by a controller, so the array as a whole decides capacity, speed and survivability.
Original 1987 term: Redundant Array of Inexpensive Disks (legacy)
Current usage: Redundant Array of Independent Disks
Proposed by Patterson, Katz, Gibson, UC Berkeley (1987)
Two core techniques: striping for parallel speed, redundancy for fault tolerance
Redundancy trades away capacity that pure striping would keep

slides.title: Heading: RAID Defined
slides.body:
Subheading: Analogy
Analogy:
A single bowler bowling every over tires out, and if injured leaves the team exposed; a team spreads overs across bowlers and keeps cover ready — just as RAID spreads data across disks and keeps redundant copies so one disk failing does not stop play.

slides.title: RAID Levels - I
slides.body: RAID Levels - I

slides.title: Heading: RAID Levels
slides.body:
Subheading: Five Standard Types
Content:
RAID levels are standard classifications defining how disks combine for performance, redundancy or both, ranging from pure striping to parity-based and nested designs.
RAID 0 uses full raw capacity, zero fault tolerance
RAID 1 mirrors data across disks
RAID 5 stripes with distributed parity
RAID 6 stripes with dual parity
RAID 10 nests striping over mirroring

slides.title: Heading: RAID 0 Striping
slides.body:
Subheading: Data Split Across Disks
Content:
RAID 0 divides a file into fixed-size stripe units and writes them across N disks in turn, so one request is served by several disks together.
Stripe unit size fixed at array setup
Data distributed round-robin across all disks
No parity or duplicate copy stored
Minimum two disks required to stripe

slides.title: Heading: RAID 0 Striping
slides.body: Subheading: Diagram

slides.title: Heading: RAID 0 Striping
slides.body: Subheading: Diagram

slides.title: Heading: RAID 0 Striping
slides.body:
Subheading: Analogy
Analogy:
Two friends split one heavy shopping list and each carry half the bags home together — just as RAID 0 splits one file across disks so both work in parallel.

slides.title: Heading: RAID 0 Performance
slides.body:
Subheading: Speed Versus Risk
Content:
Splitting one request across N disks lets all of them read or write simultaneously, so throughput scales upward — but losing any single disk destroys the whole stripe set.
Usable capacity = sum of all disk capacities
Four-disk array approaches near 4x single-disk IOPS
Failure probability rises with more disks, not falls
Best for scratch space, caches, video editing

slides.title: Heading: RAID 1 Mirroring
slides.body:
Subheading: Duplicate Copies Kept
Content:
RAID 1 keeps an identical copy of every stripe unit on a second disk, so a single drive failure leaves an untouched mirror still serving data.
Mirror set may include more than two disks for extra redundancy
Reads can be served from either mirror, boosting throughput
Failed disk replaced and resynced by direct copy, no parity math

slides.title: Heading: RAID 1 Mirroring
slides.body: Subheading: Diagram

slides.title: Heading: RAID 1 Mirroring
slides.body: Subheading: Diagram

slides.title: Heading: RAID 1 Mirroring
slides.body:
Subheading: Analogy
Analogy:
A bank keeps a signed cheque copy locked in two separate vaults so one vault's loss never loses the record — just as RAID 1 keeps identical mirrored copies on separate disks.

slides.title: Heading: RAID 1 Trade-offs
slides.body:
Subheading: Cost Versus Protection
Content:
Mirroring survives a single-disk failure without any data loss, but the protection is paid for in halved capacity and duplicated write traffic.
Usable capacity = total raw capacity divided by mirror count
Write speed limited to one disk, not parallel
Read speed can approach N times via split reads
Rebuild time depends on disk size, not stripe count

slides.title: Heading: RAID 0 Vs 1
slides.body:
Subheading: Striping Vs Mirroring
Content:
Striping and mirroring sit at opposite ends of the RAID trade-off — one maximises speed and raw capacity, the other maximises protection.

slides.title: RAID Levels - II
slides.body: RAID Levels - II

slides.title: Heading: Parity And Nested RAID
slides.body:
Subheading: Beyond Stripe Mirror
Content:
RAID 0 and RAID 1 sit at extremes of speed-only or safety-only; three further levels blend striping and redundancy in different ratios.
RAID 5: single distributed parity, tolerates one disk failure
RAID 6: dual distributed parity, tolerates two disk failures
RAID 10: mirrored pairs striped together, no parity math
All three balance capacity, speed and rebuild cost differently

slides.title: Heading: RAID 5 Parity
slides.body:
Subheading: Distributed Across Disks
Content:
RAID 5 stripes data across disks like RAID 0 but adds a parity stripe unit, computed by XOR, rotated across every disk.
Parity rotates disk to disk, no single parity drive
Any one disk failure recoverable via XOR reconstruction
Capacity = (n−1) × disk size, one disk reserved
Minimum 3 disks required

slides.title: Heading: RAID 5 Parity
slides.body: Subheading: Diagram

slides.title: Heading: RAID 5 Parity
slides.body: Subheading: Diagram

slides.title: Heading: RAID 5 Parity
slides.body:
Subheading: Analogy
Analogy:
A study group keeps one cross-check note summarising everyone else's pages; a lost notebook is rebuilt from the rest plus that note — exactly as RAID 5 recomputes a failed disk from parity on the remaining disks.

slides.title: Heading: Parity Calculation Trace
slides.body:
Subheading: XOR Reconstruction
Content:
Three data stripe units and their parity show how XOR both protects the array and rebuilds a failed disk.
Parity P = D0 XOR D1 XOR D2 (=0000)
Disk1 fails: recompute D1 = D0 XOR D2 XOR P = 1100
Write penalty: read old data + parity, XOR, write back (4 I/Os)
Full rebuild reads every surviving disk before array is safe again

slides.title: Heading: RAID 6 Dual Parity
slides.body:
Subheading: Two Disk Tolerance
Content:
RAID 6 adds a second, independently computed parity stripe unit so the array survives two simultaneous disk failures.
Second parity (Q) uses Reed–Solomon coding, not plain XOR
Tolerates any two disk failures without data loss
Minimum 4 disks required
Rebuild reads more data, so slower and costlier than RAID 5

slides.title: Heading: RAID 6 Dual Parity
slides.body: Subheading: Diagram

slides.title: Heading: RAID 6 Dual Parity
slides.body:
Subheading: Analogy
Analogy:
A hospital ward keeps both mains power and two independent backup generators on standby, so equipment keeps running even if two separate power failures strike at once — exactly as RAID 6 keeps two independent parity values so data survives any two simultaneous disk failures.

slides.title: Heading: RAID 10 Nested
slides.body:
Subheading: Mirror Then Stripe
Content:
RAID 10 mirrors pairs of disks first, then stripes data across those mirrored pairs, combining redundancy with speed.
Each mirrored pair tolerates one failure within that pair
No parity computation, so no write penalty
Minimum 4 disks, usable capacity is exactly half
Fastest rebuild: simple copy from surviving mirror

slides.title: Heading: RAID 10 Nested
slides.body: Subheading: Diagram

slides.title: Heading: RAID 10 Nested
slides.body:
Subheading: Analogy
Analogy:
Two pairs of identical twins split a trekking route between the pairs; within each pair, either twin finishes the stretch if the other falls ill — exactly as RAID 10 mirrors data within each pair while striping work across pairs.

slides.title: Heading: Comparing Three Levels
slides.body:
Subheading: Cost Versus Resilience
Content:
Choosing among RAID 5, 6 and 10 balances how much capacity is sacrificed against how many failures the array can absorb.

slides.title: Trade-offs & Reliability
slides.body: Trade-offs & Reliability

slides.title: Heading: Trade-off Dimensions
slides.body:
Subheading: Performance Cost Redundancy
Content:
Every RAID level trades three resources against each other: read/write speed, fault tolerance, and usable capacity — no level wins on all three.
Performance: throughput and IOPS for reads/writes
Redundancy: how many disk failures survive
Cost: usable capacity lost to parity/mirroring
Reliability: rebuild time and failure risk
Data protection: guarding against corruption, not just loss

slides.title: Heading: RAID Levels Compared
slides.body:
Subheading: Performance Cost Snapshot
Content:
Placing RAID 0, 1, 5, 6 and 10 side by side shows the direct trade-off between usable capacity and survivable failures.

slides.title: Heading: Rebuild Risk
slides.body:
Subheading: MTBF And Rebuild Window
Content:
Redundancy survives one failure, but rebuilding a large array after a disk swap is itself a fragile, time-consuming window.
MTBF: average operating hours between disk failures
Rebuild time grows with drive capacity and array size
Second failure during rebuild loses data on RAID 5
Unrecoverable read errors during rebuild threaten large arrays
Hot spare: idle disk that starts rebuild automatically

slides.title: Heading: Rebuild Risk
slides.body:
Subheading: Analogy
Analogy:
A single security guard covers an entire housing society gate while a second guard is still travelling to join duty, leaving the gate unchecked until the replacement arrives — exactly as an array runs unprotected during its rebuild window until a hot spare finishes copying.

slides.title: Heading: RAID Vs Backup
slides.body:
Subheading: Redundancy Not Recovery
Content:
RAID replicates every write instantly across disks, so it protects against hardware failure but cannot undo deletion, corruption, or ransomware.
Controller or firmware fault corrupts every disk alike
Silent data corruption (bit rot) can go undetected
Scrubbing: periodic read-verify pass catches corruption early
Checksum/parity mismatches flag silent errors before spread
Off-site or offline backup remains the recovery layer RAID lacks

slides.title: Heading: RAID Vs Backup
slides.body:
Subheading: Analogy
Analogy:
Photocopying a page the instant it gets torn only produces two torn copies — exactly as RAID duplicates data faithfully, damage included, which is why a separate backup is still needed.

slides.title: Heading: Choosing RAID Level
slides.body:
Subheading: Matching Use To Level
Content:
Picking a RAID level means matching its performance-cost-redundancy profile to what the workload must survive and how fast it must run.
RAID 0: scratch or temp data, speed only, no protection
RAID 1: OS/boot drives, small critical volumes
RAID 5: read-heavy file/application servers, moderate budget
RAID 6: large-capacity archives needing two-failure survival
RAID 10: databases needing speed and fast rebuild

slides.title: Heading: Section Summary
slides.body:
Subheading: Balancing Five Factors
Content:
No RAID level is universally best; each of the five levels sits at a different point on the performance-cost-redundancy-reliability spectrum.
More redundancy always costs usable capacity
Higher fault tolerance often costs write performance
Rebuild risk grows with drive size, not RAID level alone
Backup stays mandatory regardless of RAID level chosen
